item.title: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded: Following the departure of now-former NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, a new report by The Wall Street Journal (via Wccftech) has emerged alleging that NVIDIA artificially inflated the ongoing GPU and memory shortage by investing in AI startups that would go on to buy NVIDIA GPUs and build data centers. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC. The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions.The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end.

item.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
item.author: vinhnx
item.content:encoded: This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough by hand to have opinions about this.The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top.Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge.Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text.Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it.The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways.A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters ( and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time.The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS.The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the in ). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.Parts of this have been done before: in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color.: framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge.The has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. and (, and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves. terminals can outline whole input fields.What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: placement, colors, blocks, junctions, halves, styles and live. cycles the stroke width, turns borders off so you can compare, and quits. Each view also has a matching flag (, and so on) if you want to start on it.The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. and split, closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are.The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. to show and hide the boxes, and work the same as in the panes demo, and or lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the dependency.I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.

item.title: Live-migration support in FreeBSD and bhyve coming
item.author: JohnDohnBohn
item.content:encoded:
This project presents a first working state for live migration of bhyve guests on FreeBSD 15.1. A running amd64 guest can move between two hosts over TCP while continuing to run; it is paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. The work builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support and adds dirty-page tracking in the vmm kernel module together with a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.
The goal is deliberately practical: make it possible to test, discuss, and improve a real implementation rather than discuss live migration only in the abstract. The current code and test tooling are being published as a WIP RFC so that the next steps can be shaped in the open. A more detailed demonstration of a VM being live migrated can be watched on my YouTube channel.
Live migration is an important building block for enterprise virtualisation. It enables host maintenance, hardware replacement, load balancing, and failure-domain management with far less disruption to workloads. It is also central to the Sylve project, which aims to offer a Proxmox-like virtualisation solution for FreeBSD. Migration is not an optional convenience in that kind of platform; it is one of the capabilities that makes clustered operations practical.
It is equally important for BoxyBSD, where I offer free BSD-based VPS instances to individuals. Without a credible migration path, routine host work can require a guest outage. That makes live migration a current show stopper for the project, and is why this work is being pushed toward a testable, reviewable state. How the current implementation works The source starts with a pre-copy phase. It sends populated guest memory, then repeatedly obtains a bitmap of pages changed since the previous scan and sends only those pages. Once the remaining dirty set fits the configured downtime target, stops shrinking, or reaches the configured round limit, bhyve pauses the guest and its devices. It then sends the final dirty pages and the existing snapshot state for the vCPUs, kernel state, and emulated devices.
The destination validates the basic VM geometry, receives memory and state, restores it, and reports that it is ready. Only then does the source send , the commit point. Before , a failed migration can resume the source guest. The destination does not start the guest if it does not receive that commit message. A warm, stop-and-copy mode is available too, which is useful both as a fallback and as a comparison baseline. What is implemented todayPre-copy and warm migration: live pre-copy is configurable with downtime and maximum-round controls; explicit stop-and-copy migration is also supported.Multi-vCPU protocol support: the migration handshake carries the guest vCPU count, the destination refuses a count mismatch, and all guest vCPUs are paused and resumed as part of migration. The published test bed has primarily exercised a one-vCPU guest, so multi-vCPU stress and race testing remain required before making broader claims.Memory consistency checks: dirty-page tracking covers guest and mapped emulation writes through page dirty state, while vmm write holds are recorded separately. The test workload rewrites and verifies guest memory and reports any missing or stale page as a mismatch. Repeated ping-pong migrations have been used to check that the workload continues without errors. a guest-side workload repeatedly writes and fsyncs files, verifies checksums, and is checked again after a cold reboot. This is intended to exercise the device pause, drain, and restore path. destination refusal, an unreachable target, and a target disappearing during both pre-copy and stop-and-copy have been tested. Before commit, the source is intended to resume the paused guest after failure.Basic destination checks: protocol version, page size, memory layout, and vCPU count are checked before data transfer. The migration socket is opened by bhyvectl and passed into bhyve so that bhyve can remain inside its Capsicum sandbox. this is amd64-only and depends on the experimental support. It relies on snapshot-capable emulated devices; PCI passthrough is not migratablem, yet. In the current two-host test environment, repeated live migrations, memory-rewrite workloads, and fsync-heavy disk workloads have completed successfully. For a slowly dirtying 512 MiB guest, observed downtime has been roughly 138–171 ms. A rapidly dirtying guest may not converge during pre-copy, but still falls back to a correct stop-and-copy completion with a longer pause. These are encouraging engineering results, not a production support promise or a complete correctness proof. Blockers before upstreaming can be evaluated further The following are neutral engineering requirements, not criticism of the value of the prototype. They need to be addressed first before further upstreaming into FreeBSD can be evaluated responsibly. Prove and harden dirty-log correctness. The kernel-side dirty-page algorithm must be demonstrated not to lose a write while dirty bits are examined and cleared. It needs focused concurrency, paging, emulation-write, and multi-vCPU stress coverage, plus a reviewable locking and memory-ordering argument.Define a complete compatibility contract. Matching memory size and vCPU count is not enough. A destination should verify guest identity, CPU capabilities, bhyve/vmm and snapshot format compatibility, device topology and capabilities, and shared-storage identity before accepting a migration.Harden the transport and protocol. The current TCP transport has no authentication or encryption and uses a first-version native protocol. A stable protocol needs explicit wire formats, bounded message handling, timeouts, version negotiation, authentication or a supported external secure transport model, and clear operational guidance.Clarify the commit and device-side-effect boundary. The source/destination handoff must be reviewed so that device restoration cannot cause externally visible work before the source has committed, and so that the unavoidable uncertain outcome after a lost post-commit acknowledgement is operationally recoverable.Specify storage and network handoff. Shared storage must have defined coherency, durability, and fencing assumptions. Network migration also needs a clear answer for tap/bridge handling, MAC/IP movement, and traffic convergence.Build an in-tree test strategy. The current scripts and test-bed workloads are useful, but upstream review will need automated regression coverage and a documented support matrix across CPU counts, memory sizes, supported devices, host CPUs, and failure cases.Separate the work into reviewable patches. Dirty-page tracking, snapshot API refactoring, protocol/receiver work, CLI changes, and tests should be independently reviewable. This will make design feedback more actionable and reduce the risk of merging coupled changes. We have already had deeper discussions about these questions in the Sylve Discord. Publishing this current state is intended to make those discussions more concrete, bring in wider FreeBSD and bhyve feedback, and turn the prototype into a clear roadmap. The immediate focus is correctness, compatibility validation, transport safety, and repeatable tests—not adding performance features first. Currently, some peopel already have access to it and it's planned ot publish this at least as a proposal on my git and GitHub at:
Compression, zero-page elision, broader device coverage, richer orchestration, and performance tuning can follow once the foundation is sound. If you operate bhyve, work on FreeBSD virtualisation, or are interested in Sylve or BoxyBSD, testing the RFC and contributing design feedback would be especially valuable. WIP RFC for a first working bhyve live-migration implementation on FreeBSD 15.1.

item.title: No AI Slop: A Manifesto
item.author: bankombinator
item.content:encoded: Written by the speakers and attendees of AIE Code Summit 2026In 2001, 17 software engineers and leaders got together at a ski lodge in Snowbird, Utah to understand the biggest challenge of their time: heavyweight, documentation-driven software development processes.Out of this we got the Agile Manifesto, four values and twelve principles that changed how most of the industry builds software.Today we convene to build our own manifesto - the No AI Slop manifesto.AI increasingly helps us write our code, docs, plans, and messages. We've all been on the receiving end of slop, and most of us have sent some too. Through this work, we have come to value: over a model's first draft over easier work over patching the outputThe world moves especially fast these days, but the goal of these resolutions is to embrace our important human role in harnessing AI safely, responsibly, in a way that creates value for everyone, and that will be relevant for years to come.AI is the most useful tool most of us have ever worked with, but a swarm of agents can produce more work in a single day than a person can review in our lifetime.Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it.Using AI doesn't necessarily make something slop. Slop happens when we pass AI output along without taking responsibility for the quality or the reader's experience.AI cannot replace human judgement, it can only amplify our judgement (or lack thereof).Slop is asymmetric. The cost of producing a thousand-line PR or a ten-page doc is approaching zero, while the cost of reviewing it remains constant.In code, even before AI, slop proliferates when we repeatedly work around problems instead of solving them correctly. It comes from tools that lean HEAVILY toward adding rather than subtracting.A lot of slop comes from pressure. Companies are pushing their people to redefine what is humanly possible.Slop compounds. The more slop sits in our knowledge base, in chat, in code, the more of it the next agent reads and copies.The more slop flying around a team, the more we lose the will to fight it. Communication and quality get worse over time, not better.Thus we the undersigned resolve that:Human time and attention is incredibly valuable, so we optimize for using it wisely.We fight slop because AI should make our work better, not just easier.We optimize systems, tools, and products for efficient elicitation of human intent and for efficient human understanding.We do our own thinking when working with a model. We explore resources, code, and prior art to truly understand the problem before the work starts.We own the intent, taste, and consequences of what we ship, however much AI helps us make it.When an agent wrote something we're sending, we make that clear, and we check the parts that matter before it goes out.When someone sends us slop, we tell them, kindly, and ask them to review it first. Most of us have needed that same note at some point.There will always be alpha in reviewing . As models improve, we may stop reading most of the code. We may still review a plan, design, or result, because if we don't, we just get the same output as everyone else.Agent reviews, linters, and verifiers are useful but not sufficent. For now, we still review at least some subset of the outputs. What subset depends on the stakes.What shipped, who's using it, and how it's helping them matters FAR MORE than lines of code, prs merged, tokens spent, or the number of agents running in parallel.Unreviewed output isn't always necessarily bad. One-shot prompts and vibe coding are high leverage tools. "Slop" is bad when it undermines our outcome -- a useful product, a maintainable system, or saving ourselves and our teammates time and energy.When a mistake shows up twice, we scale ourselves and our team by improving the system and its guardrails. Anything a linter, type checker, or automated check can catch, we let it catch.None of us has this figured out. We're each relearning what we will and won't accept, and there's no single right answer.Again, the world moves especially fast these days, but the goal of these resolutions is to embrace our important human role in harnessing AI safely, responsibly, in a way that creates value for everyone, and that will be relevant for years to come.We look forward to working with the community to evolve these beliefs as the world changes. Comments and feedback on this document are welcome. What is slop? Why does slop happen? Why is slop worth fighting? How do we fight slop?Special thanks to Philip Kiely, Swyx, Lucas Meijer, Rebecca Bakels, Tejas Kumar, Natalie Serrino, Francisco Javier Arceo, Kent C. 的长按过程中，屏幕顶部显示进度条。HOME＋PLAY 紧急停音回起点；HOME＋SAVE 撤销／重做；SEQ＋EDIT 打开更多菜单；EDIT＋REC 改 DX7 音色名。都可以从长按 SEQ 的菜单完成对应操作。网页需要锁住按键时可 Shift 点击或右击，再点释放；日常操作无需使用。SEQ 基础页白键开关当前页的步；K3 选音高或鼓声部。PRESETS 在各参数页统一选步，SELECT 选轨，OCT−／OCT+ 每次换 16 步。ALGORITHM 翻底部八页：BASIC、STEP DETAILS、RHYTHM/REC、LOCKS、SYNC / LOOP、MIDI TRACK、MIDI ROUTING、TRACK ROLE。RHYTHM/REC 的 K4 选本轨 16／32／48／64 步，各轨独立循环。播放中修改长度会显示 节拍器（关闭／录音／常开）、K3 一小节预备拍、K4 循环长度。量化固定为十六分音符。长按 SEQ 仍保留复制、粘贴和更多操作；UNDO / REDO 在当前内容与上次编辑前状态之间切换；音色与音量到达边界后继续拧不会覆盖撤销记录。每条轨道都能选择任意一种音源，同类型的多条轨道也各有参数。切换音源后使用新类型的默认参数；鼓与旋律互换会清空不兼容步进，可从长按 SEQ 的菜单选择 UNDO / REDO 撤销。EDIT 短按开算法／反馈／移调／音量常用页，再短按返回；长按进入完整编辑。黑键选择 OP1–OP6、Pitch、Global 或 Mono／Poly，SELECT 翻页；长按 OP 黑键约半秒开关算子。ALGORITHM 调算法，PRESETS 选内置音色。短按 EDIT 调第一页；长按 EDIT 后 SELECT 翻三页：Cutoff／Reso／EnvMod／Decay；Accent／Wave／Tune／Volume；Drive／DrvTyp／Slide／AccDec。PRESETS 切换锯齿／方波，编辑页 Mono／Poly 选择单音滑音或 4 复音。PRESETS 选择 11 个鼓声部或 KIT，键盘试听也会选中对应声部。长按 EDIT 后 SELECT 翻参数页。各声部可调参数不同；KIT 不提供音高或滤波目标。FM 保留原有音高／振幅 LFO 和两页参数。效果使用 FX。EDIT 的 OP RATES／OP LEVELS 显示同一条包络：RATE 越大，对应阶段越短；LEVEL 改变折点高度。L3 保持到松键，随后按 R4 到达 L4。六个算子和 PITCH 包络均会随参数更新。图形为便于编辑的示意，不是毫秒刻度；实际时长还取决于音符、缩放与电平。FM ENV 的 A、D、S、R 录音。最小位置静音，切换项目沿用旋钮位置；它不随项目保存。转动时屏幕短暂显示 MASTER 百分比或 MASTER MUTED。在 HOME／SEQ 基础页用 K1 调当前轨。303 的 Volume、808 的声部 Level 和采样 Level 用于音色内部的平衡。按一下 GLO 进入混音，按白键 1–8 切换对应轨静音。按一下 GLO 进入混音，按白键 9–16 切换对应轨独奏。混音页中，SELECT 选轨；K1–K4 调当前四轨组（1–4 或 5–8）的音量。网页“静音”只关闭试听，编辑与音序仍继续。要停回起点，请用 HOME＋PLAY 或“紧急停音”。实机未保存的编辑只在内存中，重新开机或载入其他项目会丢失。网页与实机各有自己的存档；“保存到设备”会完成传输、写入槽位和读回校验。在 HOME 总览转 PRESETS item.title: $11.4M in Nvidia hardware vanishes during shipment from CA to TX
item.author: crescit_eundo
item.content:encoded: Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments.According to The Mercury News, the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations.Oakland police confirm investigationThe Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement:“The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.”The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded.Previous thefts involving NVIDIA productsThe Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance.In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding, from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case.

item.title: Weight Space Misfolding
item.author: mkglees
item.content:encoded: Weight space editing changes a neural network’s knowledge, behaviour and alignment through direct modification of its weights. Model-mediated weight space manipulation, also known as weight space programming or intra-weight injection, has emerged as a capability of advanced frontier models. While it offers benefits for gradient-free adaptation, it also creates an opportunity for one model to induce unauthorised behaviour in another. We call this weight space misfolding, by analogy with protein misfolding in prion disease, and consider both direct interference and hypothetical onward propagation. The asymmetry between an attacker seeking a harmful intervention, who merely needs to generate the payload attack once, and a defender who needs to find that needle in the haystack of weights, creates an impossible choice for the latter: they can either prohibit weight editing altogether, forfeiting its benefits, or be bound to cover the burden and cost. We develop a threat model and a non-exhaustive taxonomy covering factual substitution, capability denial and selective omission, including offensive uses of selective unlearning, then illustrate it on the basis of three selected case studies using the IWIBench interface. We find that while targeted disruption is possible, the limitations in reliability and functional preservation are significant. While the cases explored in this paper do not demonstrate self-propagation or actual offensive capabilities, it is abundantly clear that the building blocks are present and identifiable in frontier models. While these cases by no means directly establish self-propagation, they show why imperfect editing capabilities can still pose a security risk. We examine defensive approaches, including control of the path from authorised editing to deployment, acceptance and recovery requirements and the implications for physical AI.

item.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond
item.author: nephihaha
item.content:encoded: Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study.Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope.The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made), and so on.At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked.Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems.Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told : "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today."This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs. "When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped."Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure."Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services."This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as "permanently vulnerable." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal.And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax."What a time to be alive. ®

item.title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
item.author: halcdev
item.content:encoded: Solving long-horizon tasks without any extra trainingVanilla LeWM can be augmented to solve long-horizon physics tasks on out-of-distribution goals. This method uses transformations on a memory graph to generate on-the-fly subgoals without any additional training. Shown here are some of the hardest tasks it solved.There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [1]The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions.This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [2], a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [3], a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it.The planner is given an image like this one and has to make the scene match it. The gray T is the block, the blue disc is the robot's pusher, and the green T is the goal position painted on the table. One detail in this image turned out to affect the success rate more than replacing the predictor with simulated physics.The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are as good as perfect physics for planning.Success on 250 long-horizon tasksThat means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went.Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did.1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apartUsed exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [2] When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%.So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks.250 long-horizon tasks, goal 75 steps awayLeWM, all 75 steps at onceExact physics, all 75 steps at onceLeWM given a new subgoal every 25 stepsExact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together.LeWM's planning horizon is about 25 stepsChaining 25-step searches through subgoals keeps every search inside the range where LeWM is accurate.This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics.Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together.The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence.2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jumpLeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals.This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach.The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right?Planning through a memory of demonstrationsEach thin path is one demonstration. With free jumps, the shortest route hops between demonstrations into a path the block can't physically follow. With a cost per jump, it stays on them.The standard Push-T test is easier than it looksThe caveat is that the standard test takes a demonstration, starts the robot partway through it, and sets the goal a fixed number of steps further along the same demonstration. That's a reasonable design, but in Push-T every demonstration ends with the block in the same place. So every test goal sits on a path that demonstrations already travel, heading for the spot they all end at. For 84% of the standard test's goals, the memory graph already held a nearly identical state from another demonstration.The standard test picks its goals along these streams. The harder test asks for goals like the orange ones, which no single demonstration leads to.The usual sample is also small. On the official 50 episodes, LeWM succeeded 68% of the time with the goal 50 steps away. On 250 fresh episodes drawn the same way, it succeeded only 44%. Changing nothing but the planner's random seed flipped 38 of 250 episodes between success and failure.That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another, so the robot has to travel between states that no single demonstration connects. It only counts as a success if the block stays on target for the last 10 steps. Under these rules the memory-graph planner succeeds 75% of the time on standard tasks and 45% on the new ones. The third and fourth methods I found work on that gap.3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memoriesA memory graph is only as good as its coverage. When I deleted every stored state near the goal, success fell from 93% to 32%.Push-T has a useful symmetry here. The physics of pushing a block doesn't change if you shift, rotate or mirror the whole table. So when the graph has no states near a goal, it can take demonstration segments from elsewhere, transform them to fit the gap, and plan through those. With these transformed segments, success came back to 85%. They also stretch a small memory a long way (a graph built from 1% of the demonstrations plus transformed copies did about as well as one built from 10%).Filling a gap in memory with transformed demonstrationsBlock reached its target, 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away)On the harder test, transformed segments raise success from 45% to 56%, and they help most where demonstrations are thinnest. When the goal lies in the direction the demonstrations flow, the memory-graph planner already succeeds 69% of the time. When it lies the opposite way, plain memory gets 27% and transformed memory gets 46%.Harder test, by where the goal liesI also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. A goal has to be an image, and an image of the scene has to show the pusher somewhere, so I placed the pusher just behind the goal. In one run, the robot pushed the block to within 14 pixels of the target, close enough to count as solved. Then it pushed the block away from the goal, and kept moving the pusher toward where the pusher was in the goal image.The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations, so each one also shows where the expert’s pusher happened to be at that moment. A planner that compares its prediction with the whole goal image is trying to put the pusher there too.To measure how much this matters, I took the model out of the question. I ran the exact-physics planner twice on the same 50 tasks from the harder test, and the only difference was whether its cost included the pusher’s position as well as the block’s.Block held on target, same 50 tasksThirty tasks went from failure to success when the pusher was left out, and none went the other way. A split like that happens by chance about twice in a billion. The physics here is from the actual simulator, not predicted, so the 4x in success comes from .The planner that scored the pusher did exactly what it was asked. On the 30 tasks that flipped, it got the pusher to within half a pixel of where the goal image put it, and lost the block on the way. Placing both the T and the pusher in the exact goal position is a much harder problem to solve.Cost compares the block and the pusherCost compares the block onlyBut LeWM can’t simply be told to ignore the pusher. It scores a plan by the distance between two embeddings, and its embedding of a goal image holds the block and the pusher together, with no part labeled “pusher”. So, as a test, I measured how far a planner gets by searching over the pusher instead. It compares each prediction against 16 versions of the goal image, all with the block in the same place and the pusher moved to positions taken from stored demonstrations, and keeps the closest match. That doubled LeWM’s success on the harder test, from 11% to 23%, without retraining.Sixteen versions of one goal16 copies of the goal with the pusher moved, and the one sets the costThis applies to any robot because a goal should just be a set of end states, not a copy of an image. “Put the cup on the shelf” is solved wherever the robot’s arm ends up, but a goal image picks one arm position and makes the planner match it. A good goal accepts every end state that solves the task, and still includes what the task needs from the robot, like coming to rest at the end.The good news is that large sets of demonstrations already contain many real frames of the same object in the same place, each with the robot somewhere different. Scoring a plan against the closest of those goals allows for a larger set of valid end states to plan for.None of these four discoveries change the model's weights. They apply to LeWM as published, and they should carry over to larger JEPA world models that plan the same way, at no extra training cost.The biggest open problem remaining is generalizing to tasks that don't have perfect demonstrations. On the harder Push-T test, the best planner holds the block on target 56% of the time, and most of the remaining failures are goals that run against the direction of the data. Closing that gap needs a higher level that can propose its own subgoals beyond the demonstrations, and do it better than today's learned hierarchies like H-JEPA [4], which so far match or slightly beat flat LeWM on Push-T.Hierarchical subgoal planner on top of LeWMGoing in, I assumed LeWM's predictions would be the bottleneck, but a JEPA small enough to train in a few hours already predicts about as well as the simulator itself, and there are several gains that can be achieved simply by changing the way it plans. What it can't do yet is choose its own subgoals where no demonstration has been. That's what I'm currently working on, and if you want to see more, I'll post about it first on X, @haddyalchaer.

item.title: AI unlocks Gödel's notebooks, said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
item.author: bookofjoe
item.content:encoded: The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: [incorrect] or [bad].”Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

item.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
item.author: kamaraju
item.content:encoded: Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework."Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry." Related Story: NPRBut even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search."The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.The "AI or nothing" approachIn any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois. Related Story: NPR"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging."Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

item.title: Minnesota guitarist's "palmfrets" invention strikes a new chord
item.author: bookofjoe
item.content:encoded: FERGUS FALLS — The back room of Stella’s restaurant in Fergus Falls filled with people on Oct. 28, all there to see musician Ben Ranson play.Ranson, who grew up in Sebeka, Minnesota, and currently lives in Sandstone, is a regular performer at venues across the region, including in Fergus Falls. But Oct. 28 was no ordinary gig. That night, Ranson revealed something he’d been working on for years.It wasn’t a new song or a clever guitar lick, it was an invention called “palmfrets” — something Ranson believes could change the way guitarists use their instrument. It allows players to play new bass lines or melodies using their palm, a special set of frets called palmfrets and a technique called palmfretting. The idea for palmfrets came to Ranson over five years ago.Ranson had already been doing musical experiments — even constructing organ-like foot pedals and learning the seven string guitar — all in a quest to get more notes out of the guitar, specifically more bass notes.He said the reason behind the invention, initially, was entirely artistic. He wasn’t thinking much about developing a commercial product.“That was not on my mind at all,” Ranson said. “And it wasn’t really until I made one that really worked that it sort of dawned on me like, oh, this is something that people are really going to want.”Ranson made an early-stage version of the invention in his garage, and said that, at first, he didn't recognize the importance of what he had created. He set it aside and left it in a corner for awhile — years, even.Eventually, he returned to his forgotten creation. It was then that he began to hear the music.He drafted his ideas and designs on paper, and enlisted the help of engineers. Together, they created new prototypes made from 3D printed plastic and laser-cut metal parts.It was during that time when Ranson said something shifted.“It hit me, like, I’ve really done it.”Ranson knew the plastic and metal version was not practical, and only lasted a matter of weeks. But it worked, and from there, Ranson said the engineering became more serious.Serious enough that Ranson applied for a patent, which he received on Oct. 6, 2026.Ranson had an inkling that this was something special, and recalled the first time he started playing the guitar with a solid prototype.“I was like, ‘I’m doing things that Chet Atkins never did,’” he joked. “I just had this sort of realization, like, other people are going to want to do this.”Fast forward to Oct. 28 in Fergus Falls, and Ranson’s invention is now in the hands of other guitar players.Using the pisiform bone — a small, pea-shaped bone in the wrist, near the bottom of the palm — players depress a string on the palmfret, an extra fret or set of frets near the wrist of the picking hand. The player can then use the thumb of their picking hand to pluck the string fretted by the pisiform bone.This frees up the fretting hand — the hand which frets strings on the neck of the guitar — meaning the player can move up and down the fret board more freely, and fret other strings because the pisiform bone is doing some of the hard work.“So if you want to, you can move (the fretting hand) anywhere you want, play any other notes that you want to play,” said Ranson.Essentially, guitarists could play a bass line with their pisiform bone and play other melodies or chords that would have otherwise been, literally, out of reach.Ranson had some rules when designing palmfrets.“One of the basic principles in inventing it has been: if it interferes with the normal way that you would play the guitar, it’s no good,” he said.“So the basic principle is you have to keep all of the function of the guitar as people know it,” he explained. “It has to add, but it can’t take away. That’s the basic principle.”Still, adding another element to the guitar introduces a learning curve, even for players as skilled as Ranson.He gave proof of the learning curve by showing a callus on his pisofone bone — a callus reminiscent of the ones beginning guitarists get on their fingers when first learning to play — and compared his skill-level with the palmfrets to being a teenager playing in their first band and only knowing six songs.“That is the stage I am at now, frankly.”During the reveal, other guitar players tested out the palmfrets, taking turns passing around acoustic guitars, electric, and even the bass.Darren Quam, a musician from Battle Lake, who was in attendance on Oct. 28, tried his hand — or palm — at the new invention.“At first, you know, it took me a second to kind of understand how you could use it,” Quam said. “But then — especially when Ben had us come up and try it — then, you know, trying it with my own hands, I was like, okay, I see how this could be very useful in certain situations.”Quam also commented on the learning curve. “It’s not a whole new instrument, but it’s a whole new way of playing.”Despite the new way of playing, during the reveal show, Quam seemed to catch on quickly, with Ranson joking “we’re going to have to take this away from you.”From a practical standpoint as a gigging musician, Quam thought the invention would be useful for solo players.“I think it really is probably the most useful in like a solo situation where you’re playing and you can accompany yourself, especially with those lower notes where you can fret with your palm hand and change the root note or the chords, and still be able to have the freedom to play on the higher strings as if there was someone else accompanying you, you know, like a bass player.“So it’s kind of like you’ve got a bass player on your palm all of a sudden.”And speaking of bass players, Ranson believes the bass guitar, as it now is, could become “obsolete.”“But for a great reason, as far as bassists are concerned,” he said.With the palmfrets, a bass player could play a bass line beneath a bass line, or play chords while playing a bass line. Meaning a bass player could accompany themselves, or add chords when playing with a group.“As a guitarist, you might want to play some jazz song, or whatever song you want — it’s got a clear melody, but you just need to have chords underneath it so that people can understand what that melody is.”With palmfrets, the bass player can play the chord and the bass line, rooting the listener, while allowing the lead guitarist to focus on the melody.Ranson explained that he expects the invention to make the bass into a very powerful instrument, “kind of like a piano.”For Ranson, thinking about how the invention will be used in the future is all speculation.“But I think it’s going to be really interesting. I mean, I can’t wait,” said Ranson.The true potential of the invention, according to Ranson, might not be revealed for many years.“Let’s say 15 years from now, there’s going to be some kid who got one of these as a teenager. Then you’ll know what it can do.”

item.title: Why Zig over C for Systems Programming
item.author: torutofu
item.content:encoded: After I wrote Why Zig Over Rust for Systems Programming, the obvious next question was C. The Rust question was about safety and how much ceremony I was willing to accept for it. The C question is different, because Zig and C want the same things. Both are small languages without a Garbage Collector and both stay close to what the machine does. So this post is not about leaving C for something completely different. It is about the parts of C that cost me time and how Zig deals with them. All the code was compiled on a Mac with Zig 0.17 and clang.C is the language of UNIX. The kernels, the C libraries and most of the system libraries that every other language calls in the end are written in C and the man pages describe them with C prototypes and C examples. A C program from the 1990s still compiles today and there is a C compiler for almost every CPU that was ever made. The language is small enough that one book, The C Programming Language by Kernighan and Ritchie, covers all of it. Zig itself does not try to replace any of that. It talks to C libraries directly and it uses the C ABI when it needs to. I am not writing this post because I think C is bad; C is my favorite programming language! I am writing it because I do not want to write new code in C any more.The C code that I like the least is a function that acquires several resources and has to release them in reverse order when something fails halfway. The usual answer, which is also the one the Linux kernel uses, is :It works, but the cleanup is far away from the allocation and the order of the labels has to match the order of the allocations by hand. The same function in Zig looks like this:Each sits right below the allocation it undoes and runs only if the function returns an error. Zig runs them in reverse order, so there are no labels to keep in order. What I like even more is that I can test every failure path. The std.testing.FailingAllocator type fails on the first, second or third allocation, depending on the value of . The testing allocator below it reports any memory that is not freed:Testing the same three paths in the C version needs a wrapper around or an external tool.In C an array that goes to a function becomes a pointer and the length travels separately, if at all. The following C function has an off-by-one error, instead of :With an array of it prints on my Mac and exits with 0. The extra 1 came from whatever was in memory after the array. Neither clang with nor the program itself complains. In Zig a slice carries its length, so the same mistake stops the program in the and modes:In real Zig code you would write and the mistake cannot happen at all. Strings work the same way. A Zig string is a slice of bytes with a length, so there is no call that walks the memory looking for a 0 byte and no buffer that is one byte short because somebody forgot the terminator.In C a function reports an error by returning -1 or and setting , or by returning an error code, or in some other way that the man page describes. Nothing forces you to check. A lot of C code calls and without looking at the return value and the compiler is fine with it. In Zig an error is part of the return type and the compiler refuses to compile a call whose error you ignore. You have to use , or . The failure path is in the source code, right next to the call, which is also what I liked about Go.The C preprocessor works with text and knows nothing about C. The classic #define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b)) evaluates one of its arguments twice and a big C project usually has a lot of lines for every Operating System it supports. In Zig, code that runs at compile time is ordinary Zig code. Instead of I write if (builtin.os.tag == .linux) and the compiler drops the branch that does not apply. Generic data structures are functions that take a type and return a type. The compiler checks all of it like the rest of the program. I wrote about this in Zig comptime.In C the overflow of a signed integer is undefined behavior. The following C program adds 1 to :Compiled with clang it prints and exits with 0, but the C standard allows the compiler to do anything, including removing code that it decides can never run. In Zig the overflow of any integer, signed or unsigned, is checked in the and modes and the program stops with and the line where it happened. When I want wrapping, I write and when I want the result to stop at the maximum value, I write .The command is a C compiler that you can use instead of or . It also cross compiles out of the box. On my Mac, zig cc -target x86_64-linux-musl -o sum sum.c creates a static Linux executable without installing anything else. In the mode also turns on the undefined behavior sanitizer, so the program above compiled with stops with panic: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'. A file can compile C files next to Zig files, so you can move a C project to Zig one file at a time and keep using the same build. If your Zig code needs C header files, Zig 0.17 removed and you use instead. I wrote about that in @cImport() Is gone in Zig 0.17.Zig is not C with all the problems solved. It does not stop you from using memory after you free it or from keeping a pointer to a stack variable that no longer exists. In the and modes most safety checks are turned off and you are back to undefined behavior, just as in C. C is also stable in a way that Zig is not yet. When Zig 0.17 came out, I had to change 35 of the 152 Zig files of my book, while C code from decades ago still compiles. C has more tools, more books, more people who know it and compilers for chips that Zig does not support. If you write code for a microcontroller that only has a vendor C compiler, the choice is made for you.C is not going away and I still read a lot of it, because the UNIX source code and most system libraries are written in C and their man pages document them with C prototypes. But for new code I choose Zig. It lets me write the same kind of code as C, close to the machine and with no runtime, while the compiler and the mode catch many of the mistakes that C lets through without a word.

item.title: The Dawn of the Data Intelligence Engineer
item.author: jonbaer
item.content:encoded: Something is different this timeBefore December 2025, the case against AI for analytics was easy to make. LLMs wrote bad SQL. Business logic was unknowable. The sensible conclusion was that this was never going to work. In fact, I used to talk about how data teams were more or less exempt from the disruption that was happening in other areas of software.Then, all of a sudden, the ground moved. New models got better at SQL. Business logic turned out to be something an agent can figure out with some helpful context. And agents went multi-turn, which means they don't have to get it right the first time. They can try a query, look at what came back, and try again, just like a human analyst would do. Put those together and it … just … works.Self-service BI has been right around the corner for decades, what makes this different? Well, as a bit of an existence proof, here’s an example; the presentation I gave at Data Outpost was not created as a powerpoint deck or Google Slides, it was an app that I built using MotherDuck and Claude. I used live datasets from four different data sources, built a number of interactive and animated visualizations. Anything I did could be done by virtually anyone; I didn’t look at a single line of code or SQL.It is important to stress that this isn’t just a way to automate building your dashboards. BI is typically pretty static, with maybe a couple of drill-downs. But with AI, you can build much richer visualizations. And what’s more, if you can build a dashboard with a prompt, you can go beyond that and also build a full-blown app.Allowing business stakeholders to answer questions with data on their own has an even broader benefit than just shortening the data team’s backlog; it actually allows them to make better decisions. By cutting down the amount of time it takes and the number of handoffs involved, they can ask more questions. They can ask follow up questions while they still have all of the context in their heads. This means they can make confident decisions faster.

item.title: Global Microsoft Outage
item.author: TechTechTech
item.content:encoded:
After hours of disruption affecting millions of users worldwide, Outlook and other Microsoft services are finally returning to normal.
Microsoft has apologized for the outage, which could end up costing billions in lost productivity.
The company reported “encouraging recovery progress” saying that queues of emails waiting to be delivered are “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Any of the applications involving email or Microsoft’s Exchange Online Services were affected, the company said. That left users likely unable to access or send new emails, use Microsoft’s AI tool Copilot, or join pre-scheduled Teams meetings already in the calendar. Other services — like those that share documents, pool a company’s data or protect emails — might also have been affected. The outage left millions without the work tools they use every day and could cost $7 billion in lost productivity, according to an estimate by a Michigan think tank. Patrick Anderson, Anderson Economic Group’s president, said that perhaps as many as 26 million users on Thursday and 51 million users on Friday have actually seen their operations disrupted in a way that caused an economic loss. And he said the cost will likely increase beyond this initial estimate. City governments across the US reported disruption, encouraging residents to call local offices if necessary. Some Brits experienced delays in getting their drug prescriptions and several UK police forces told the public to report crimes or issues by telephone rather than through their websites.
Meanwhile, bank workers in Hong Kong had their work disrupted, government employees in Japan resorted to creating physical copies of documents and courts in the Philippines were hindered by the outage. Some railway networks experienced disruption to their customer email services and routing schedules while Australian schools, courts and government services reported disruption. Microsoft said the outage was caused by a “technical issue” rather than any cybersecurity breach. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.
