item.title: Dwarf planet candidate appears which takes roughly 280 years to orbit our sun
item.author: cybermango
item.content:encoded:
Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big.Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.”Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić. They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became.“We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks, he says.The object, called 2026 ED138, is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system.“This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne, a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.”Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides. But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.)Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet
Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions. ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger.Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says.Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light.Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.”Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.”The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds.What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Atacama Desert.“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision,” Jurić says in a statement.“I was surprised that it found such an object so early,” Megan Schwamb, a planetary scientist at Queen’s University Belfast in Northern Ireland and a member of the Rubin solar system operations team, tells CNN’s Jacopo Prisco. “This was not on my bingo card for this year.”Understanding more about how and where ED138 formed could reveal new details about the early days of the solar system. And its existence offers a clear reminder that surprising objects remain to be found on the fringes of our planetary neighborhood.“Is there a Mars- or Earth-size or bigger object out there?” Holman says. “That’s not ruled out.”

item.content:encoded: Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with OrchestratorEarlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation.Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new tier.Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text.Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business.

item.author: mbStavola
item.content:encoded: The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.If you have a previous version of Rust installed via , you can get 1.100.0 with:If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel () or the nightly channel (). Please report any bugs you might come across!After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, ! This also completes the project goal for this work.The never type, spelled in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as , , and , also have the type .Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a or an :While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:Additionally this release changes to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used be compatible with using . This was the plan ever since the introduction of and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).Unfortunately, to allow changing , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from to in editions 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently and . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized trait.This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!: run a closure on every exit pathThe trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we , , or panic. being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.Implementing can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped. takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements and so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable. also implements a associated function which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure: Conjuring zero-sized typesAs Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.Instead of transmuting , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init(), or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition. Reporting unused dependencies in CargoBuilding dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every in a package when only some may use it.Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running won't show warnings for unused because another may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built. Reducing Cargo cache collisionsCargo builds all libraries and binaries in the and then uplifts final artifacts to the . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a across git worktrees.The now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases. Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldownsMalicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:The newer version will be recorded in and kept from then on until a later re-resolves it.A few things to keep in mind:This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a field in the index are never held back. ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with if needed.Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

item.content:encoded: If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed.Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core.In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL.I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability. I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile. This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story.During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was . That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future.What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution.This was my first time meeting with things like , etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind:How does PostgreSQL itself decide what a value is? And how does it process and represent it?Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core.Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23. I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337?While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types.The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree.Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the ? why has and where is my value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types. Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named taught me these:constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize:On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first:So had not disappeared. But why do we even have [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ?That was because was not declared as an . It was declared as a , which was Our value value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier.How can that same 8-byte represent a , an , or custom types ?A Datum Does Not Know What It IsChatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents.The eight bytes carrying did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this .That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the system catalogThat means the row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the type ?For text, means that the representation have a variable length. And means that the Datum carried a pointer.So the same value stores a memory address for the text. Datum can pass the value either by value itself or by reference to it. Nice, I love the elegant abstraction Datums provides!So far everything makes sense, but I wanted to better understand the and columns too. These functions convert the value provided by the query into a native Datum or vice versa. So I ran this again.But then I added quotation marks to see if PostgreSQL has dynamic type casting/recognition or something:I was a bit confused at this moment. I initially thought unknown meant “PostgreSQL does not know the type.” So I went back to chatting with my pg_expert agent, who is teaching me everything so far. I learned that is an actual PostgreSQL type with , used for string literals whose final type hasn’t been decided yet!Again, this makes super sense because PostgreSQL deliberately assigns untyped string literals this temporary type because the same text could eventually become many different things!For example, the query supplies the target type int4. PostgreSQL looked up the function for and called and when its need to be printer it use Critical Thinking: Wait a Minute! The Type Chooses the CodeUp until this point, typinput and typoutput looked like ordinary conversion mechanism to me. contained many different native functions for many different types.While learning more about these functions, one detail stayed with me. An output function did not inspect a Datum and discover its type. It simply trusted all the values and flags around the Datum. extracted an integer because PostgreSQL had already selected it as the output function for . A different output function could interpret the same generic carrier according to completely different rules.I still remember that, at that very moment, I was actually thinking about the TOCTOU Vulnerabilities class of the web apps I have been exploiting/fixing for years and years.“What if I could somehow change the type between the moment PostgreSQL constructed a value and the moment it used that value?”If I can do this, we might be able to force PostgreSQL to process a Datum created for a completely different type as if it were the type the function expects. Having a type confusion in PostgreSQL can actually give me an opportunity to abuse all the other functions in PostgreSQL internals.So I went back to learning more about what I can use to force PostgreSQL to natively call different types’ output functions for my int4 value. It turns out that the feature can be used for that purpose.LANGUAGE internal: Type Confusion I Could Create on PurposeThe LANGUAGE internal allows a to create an SQL function pointing to native code already compiled into PostgreSQL. I created the following one.Then I gave it the same int4 value. and my local-backend crashed!I’m pretty sure the PostgreSQL experts reading this wouldn’t be surprised by this crash, but it surprised me a lot!It sent me in a completely different direction. I built a working exploit using this type-confusion feature to exploit against security extensions deployed by managed PostgreSQL providers. That research eventually became a part of the Part 2 story.For a while, I moved on and left this type-confusion question behind.Roughly two weeks later, something completely unrelated brought me back to it.Detour: Tomatoes and SQL InjectionLet me take a small detour. This Postgres article series is all about telling you my story in the end, isnt it ?I do not remember the exact date, but during one of our runs or walks, my partner Bilge (Staff Machine Learning Engineer at EDB) and I were discussing second-order SQL injection in the PostgreSQL AI extensions and the possibility of tricking AI features of these extensions to hallucinate and produce malicious SQL queries.That conversation led to chatting about .I first learned about SQL injection around 2005, and God knows how many times I have exploited it since.Twenty years later, most libraries and frameworks still rely heavily on string escaping to generate secure SQL queries, even though RDBMSs have a beautiful feature named prepared statements.I studied them when I was a uni student, mostly to see what could still be exploited even if the target app uses prepared statements. Things like triggering excessive SQL cold parsing and stuff like that.But more importantly, for years I taught SQL Injection to thousands of my trainees with this concept:“Knowledge is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is not putting it in a fruit salad.”In my version, the SQL query is the recipe and the values are the ingredients. Prepared statements let the database understand the recipe first, then receive the ingredients separately. So even a value like may look evil, but it remains data and never gets the chance to rewrite the query.I had always seen this separation as a security feature. But this time, I noticed something in the middle of the convo with Bilge. Databases can finish all the parsing first and wait for me to execute it. Before execution, I can run whatever query I want.I can alter types before executing the query!Uncovering 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion PrimitiveSo the idea is simple; I could prepare a query, change something, and execute it later. But change what? PostgreSQL is not gonna let me redefine what the built-in types , , or mean.I was not thinking about composite types at this point. Honestly, I barely knew what they were. I asked Claude agent pg_expert a much simpler question:Which PostgreSQL types can I create, use inside a prepared query, and then alter it before running execute ?That question led me to composite types. In PostgreSQL, a composite type represents the structure of a row. It is essentially a custom, user-defined data type that acts as a container for multiple fields, each with its own name and data type. [1, 2]It had its own type OID, but its attributes defined the current row layout. I can change the attribute a type from UUID to another type without replacing the composite type itself.I created a one-field composite where the attribute started as UUID. Then I prepared a query, changed that attribute to bytea, and executed the prepared statement.And the result was a segfault!I knew I had found exactly the kind of type confusion I had been looking for!I knew this was no longer a superuser-only LANGUAGE internal behaviour I had exploited before.I knew that I could trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role on any PostgreSQL instance. Probably all the Postgres-compatible offerings too (more about this later)Last but not least, I already knew that controlled bytes reaching the wrong native consumer, in my case, had serious exploitation potential. These two have the most reliable exploit primitive I have seen in the PostgreSQL exploits.Before diving into the Hacking PostgreSQL internals, we need to learn a few things about PostgreSQL to better understand the rest of the article!Quick Course: What is BYTEA ? is PostgreSQL’s data type for storing arbitrary binary data. Internally, it uses a variable-length representation called . PostgreSQL places a small header before the bytes to describe their size and storage format.The header tells PostgreSQL which representation it is looking at and how large the complete value is.We do not need to understand every representation. For the rest of this article, we only need to know two thingsFor example, a normal inline example of the five ASCII characters . That 24 can be decoded as which is 9. So 4-byte header + 5-byte payload = 9 bytes!The most important example, external representation, when header starts with PostgreSQL believes the value is not stored inline at all. Instead, it treats the bytes as a reference to an expanded object somewhere in memory.So the following data after the header is just object reference pointer instead of the data itself.Crash and Root Cause AnalysisLets get back to where we were.The UUID I supplied contained exactly sixteen bytes, starting with and . While attribute a was still UUID, there was nothing special about or the fourteen zero bytes following it. They were simply controlled UUID data. changed the current definition of attribute from to , but it did not convert or rewrite the binary value already stored by the prepared query. During , PostgreSQL still had exactly the same bytes.When we EXECUTE the query, PostgreSQL need to return the value of our type pg_temp.poc, in order to do that, it calls the composite output function, record_out().So looks at the pg_temp.poc’s attribute and says ‘That is bytea’ and selects But the data takes is our old UUID bytes that we can control. This is where the type confusion happens!All of these means, we can literally create any representation we want by fully controlling the headers and following 12 byte!PostgreSQL thinks it needs to reach the ExpandedObjectHeader but its address is 00000000 because thats what we have written inside the UUID, therefore local-backend crash.Before could print the value, it first needed to convert this external representation into something it can print. I learned that PostgreSQL calls this process .When we run , the call path is as follows. The relevant path looked like thisPostgreSQL then passed the pointer to . The important line inside that function was effectively: is what we influence and we choose 00000000 in our POC, which is a NULL. Therefore PostgreSQL crashed while trying to read its pointer because it believed it had received a valid external expanded object and followed the normal code path to process it.The exploitation idea: replacing NULL with our fake object that could make PostgreSQL follow to our own choosen methods!Hijacking control-flow via Fake ExpandedObjects contains Native Function PointersExpandedObjectMethods contains two native function pointersNormal code uses those methods like this to convert an expanded object into its flat representation whenever it’s needed.This is not normally an attacker-controlled callback interface. These are trusted internal representations created by PostgreSQL. The output functions can assume the pointer, header, and methods table are not malicious.These are indirect native function calls. PostgreSQL obtains the function addresses from the object’s methods table and then calls them. That is something we can actually use to change the control-flow path.Before going further, I needed a simple model for the objects involved. I named the two fake objects according to what they representedSo our plan is that the pointed to , pointed to , and contained the native function addresses that we wanna cal.The important detail is that PostgreSQL used twice. Lets remember the actual C codeFirst, it treated as an and read the pointer at offset .That pointer led to , where we had placed the address of . PostgreSQL then called the selected method and passed the original object pointer, , as its first argument.In other words, H helped PostgreSQL find , and then the same H was handed to as its parameter.Fortunately, the first eight bytes of H came before the pointer. I could place the NULL-terminated command in those bytes while keeping the address of at offset . Leaking Memory Addresses and defeating the ASLR with the same primitiveAs I have heavily talked about exploiting extensions vulnerabilities on managed-Postgres providers at Part 1, we dont get to read due to hardening. Our exploitation plan is very clear but the challenge is we need to leak addresses of these objects. I started to chatting with my to find more about PostgreSQL operation that could return a pointer-valued data while SQL expected an ordinary integer. The moment I prompted the agent, it went to“Oh actually we have talk about this during pg_clickhouse exploit back in July. Do you remember the ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL Array ?”– my beloved teacher pg_expert agentIt was a twist of fate. I had ended up exactly where the original idea had started. store their element type inside their binary representation. trusts that internal type when deciding how to extract each element. Normally, everything agrees:The says its element is , so returns a pointer-valued text Datum and SQL processes it as text.But what if the array internally says , while the surrounding SQL contract says ?Because is passed by reference, returns a Datum containing the memory address of the text value! But the surrounding SQL expression expects a by-value , so PostgreSQL prints those same pointer bits as an integer.In other to say this, we can exploit exactly same type confusion vulnerability to alter the arrays’ text element type to bigint so that unnest() will return the memory address instead of the value! aka leaking memory address!Creating a PostgreSQL Array data structures with UUID The smallest PostgreSQL Array needs 48 bytes. A single UUID gives a 16 controlled bytes. So we can simply combine 3 UUIDs next to each other to build exactly 48 byte fully controlled data structer!The animation above shows how three UUIDs become one 48-byte array carrier. I prepare those bytes while all three attributes are still UUIDs. From there, I exploit the same type confusion for only the first UUID to ! So extracts the element as and returns its pointer, while SQL expects a and exposes that pointer as a memory address. The final skips the text header and lands on my controlled payload.A direct to confusion would only reinterpret the old text bytes as an integer. The array was important because it forced PostgreSQL to first produce a real pointer and then expose those same pointer bits as a .Full working exploit on PostgreSQL 18.6CVE-2026-6460 Umbrella Fix and Variant Analysis of 21 more casesOnce I have reached that point, I started thinking about different scenarios of where we can alter the attribute types before execution. All the other possible ways of keeping the old value alive.I found the same underlying mistake around , conversion caches and different places. I reported in total.9 November 2026 The PostgreSQL security commits landed as part of a much larger release containing 52 new CVE. are directly connected to this article. is the main umbrella fix for type confusion. It introduces composite attribute versioning, anonymous RECORD descriptors. backend-local anonymous-RECORD typmod statistics import could publish values under an obsolete type prevents ExecEvalFieldStore[De]Form from using a mismatched integer overflow in tuple-size calculationCoordinating this with managed-PostgreSQL ProvidersThe reason why I have fallen into that rabbit hole 5 months ago was because I needed to better understand the how managed-database industry works before making a decision because at the end of the day, we all can outsource the infrastructure but we can not outsource the risk. When the vulnerability belongs to PostgreSQL core, how does the industry coordinate to protect its own customers?So I ported the my locally working exploit to almost every managed PostgreSQL platform I know and privately shared reproducible PoCs with their security teams. I haven’t seen any vendor who is not affected by this vulnerability! including those who has Postgres compatible offering. security team engineers validated all the exploits immediately. Thanks to Aaron and his team. Google escalated the reports to its highest priority P0. I am genuinely grateful of all the support from Google Cloud VRP team since day one! team received the full details around mid August. Thanks to endless support from the Etienne since I first contacted him.Ubicloud members reached out to me after my part 1 article published and then they introduced me with the ClickHouse team. Both parties are also read in somewhere at end of August. and Microsoft Azure PostgreSQL teams received the reports and working PoC at mid August.But what I respected the most is that some vendors brought their most senior engineering members to start implementing their own mitigation. They did not want to leave customers exposed while waiting for the upstream release cycle. So yeah my whole August was like that.Closing: Thank you PostgreSQL Communities and Core Security TeamI spent 20 years of my life around security communities around the globe. But I really need to say that the support, positive approach and the respect I have seen my time at PGCONF.eu this year was quite suprized me. Have no idea PostgreSQL community at europe has such a family kind vibe. After my talk “Nobody Gets to Be Superuser (Until I Broke In)” at PGCONF.eu last month Valencia, I have received amazing support from everyone, specially the respected members of the community who are effortlessly fixing these vulnerabilities whenever someone sends an email to the securit@ address. I owe so much of where I am today to open source. I’ve spent my life learning by hacking things, understanding how they work, and making them more secure. Being able to contribute to PostgreSQL and its ecosystem in my own way means a lot to me. Seeing those contributions so warmly welcomed means even more. My talk this year was not recorded upon my request, but I receive a lot of invitation from different countries for their local PostgreSQL meetups. If you’d like to hear the whole story, I’ll be presenting the 90 minutes edition of it at the Prague PostgreSQL Meetup on Monday, 30 November.(If you’ve made it this far, I’d love to hear your thoughts! item.title: Our software engineering interviews are changing a little
item.author: maitland
item.content:encoded: Over the last few years, LLMs have changed how software gets built and that’s no different for us at Jane Street. Most of our engineers now use them every day not only for writing code, but also for reading, debugging, and reviewing code, and plenty of things that aren’t code at all.Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go.That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our interviews should evolve, too. As generating code has become arguably cheaper than ever, other parts of the job have come to matter even more: taste about what to build, choosing abstractions that last, and making sure what got built is actually correct, among other things.So this summer we started trialing some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus candidates. Broadly, they involve less code-writing, and lean more higher-level, focusing on software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code, and on using LLMs to produce code. Most rounds will continue to be traditional coding interviews, conducted without LLM assistance.We know this sounds vague, but that’s intentional: the formats are still evolving, and we’d rather not describe something in detail today that looks different in six months.A few things worth knowing:Not every onsite includes these new rounds yet, and when you come on-site we’ll give you a heads-up about what to expect.While we find LLMs incredibly valuable as part of our daily work, we also recognize that not everyone has deep experience working with them. You shouldn’t feel like you need to have a highly worked out methodology for working with agents in order to do well in our process. In the end, we’re looking for people with great instincts for building software, and we don’t feel like we need an LLM to evaluate that.Different folks have integrated LLMs into their workflows in different ways and to different degrees, and we don’t expect you to have a particular setup or to use them for everything. What we care about is that you think clearly about the tools you use: what they’re good at, where they fall short, and when to reach for something else.As has been the case for some time, our more experienced candidates’ interviews will continue to be more varied, featuring a range of interview styles, from producing software to designing systems and discussing prior work.As always, we’ll keep iterating, and we’ll write more when there’s more to say.

item.title: Researchers discover rare star system that emits radio signals every 8 minutes
item.author: giuliomagnifico
item.content:encoded: Scientists at the Curtin University node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun.The newly discovered system, known as GPM J071507−114153, consists of two stars orbiting each other: a white dwarf — the dense core left behind when a star dies — and a G-type star similar to our own Sun.It is the first time radio pulses have been detected from a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star. Typically, such pulses are observed in systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars, meaning the discovery breaks new ground.These types of stellar pairs belong to a broader class of objects known as long-period transients (LPTs), producing radio signals that switch on and off over intervals ranging from minutes to hours. Around a dozen have been detected since the first was discovered by the same ICRAR team in 2021, and astronomers are still working to understand them.While several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and another star, it has remained unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses.“This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” said lead author and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, Dr Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. The team processed more than 100 hours of radio data at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre to validate and understand the white dwarf motion.Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, co-author on the paper, said that the pulses emitted by the white dwarf allowed the team to detect stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to those that create aurorae here on Earth.“As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.”“It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.”ICRAR researchers have been at the forefront of discovering these rare systems.“We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.After the LPT was located using the radio telescopes, the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star through optical observations.Both the MWA, led by Curtin University at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia, and MeerKAT, built and operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in the country’s North Cape province, serve as precursors for the SKA telescopes, SKA-Low in Australia and the SKA-Mid in South Africa, respectively.Dr McSweeney said, “If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.”

item.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server
item.author: soheilpro
item.content:encoded: A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild. CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.Specifically, the flaw exists within the function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version or later. This release addresses the race condition in .Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than .2. Implement Temporary MitigationsIf immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.Edit the configuration file (such as ) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

item.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
item.author: herpderperator
item.content:encoded: United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as and to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances."As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group. "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app. United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline.""But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

item.title: The Utah Teapot
item.author: cobbal
item.content:encoded: The has been the symbol of computer graphics. It was one of the first computer graphics models created using Bézier patches. This is the official Utah Teapot page, where you can you can visualize and download any of these historical versions or customize it, using the settings above. Terms of Use and Attribution:The Utah Teapot model files are freely available for any use, including commercial use. To preserve the historical identity and provenance of the model, users are requested to identify the model, and any substantially derived version of it, as a (or ) and to acknowledge its origin as the historic Utah Teapot developed at the University of Utah. This request is intended solely to preserve the historical identity of the Utah Teapot and is not intended to restrict use of the model. The model files are provided “as is,” without warranty of any kind. The provider of these files shall not be liable for any claims, damages, or other liability arising from their use.The Utah Teapot was originally created by Martin Newell and went through a number of modifications over the years. It quickly became famous within the graphics community after making its first appearance at SIGGRAPH in 1976. Its extensive use in graphics prompted Arvo and Kirk [1987] to name it the “Teapotahedron” and jokingly call it “the sixth Platonic solid”. It remains one of the standard models for evaluating new computer graphics algorithms and frequently appears in technical papers presented at SIGGRAPH and other graphics conferences. Utah Teapot has also appears in art installations, movies, video games, and a wide range of other graphics applications. Versions of the Utah Teapot model are included in numerous rendering and modeling programs and graphics APIs, among them 3ds Max, Direct3D, Houdini, Modo, OpenGL, POV-Ray, Quartz Composer, and RenderMan. See the Wikipedia page on the Utah Teapot.Version 1975 - Martin Newell This is the original version created by Martin Newell, while he was a PhD student at the University of Utah, by approximating the proportions of a physical teapot (Melitta by Friesland Porzellan). It is formed by 28 cubic Bézier patches, which he first drew the control points on an engineering paper. It is one of the first computer graphics object modeled using a set of nonlinear surfaces, rather than a collection of polygons. Notably, Martin Newell's version is taller than the commonly known shape of the famous Utah Teapot, and it has no bottom. This is the model that appeared in his dissertation, titled “The utilization of procedure models in digital image synthesis” in 1975, along with the rest of the tea set he modeled, though he prepared these models earlier, sometime in 1974.Martin Newell's drawing of the Teapot and the tea set image from his dissertation.Jim Blinn, while he was a PhD student at the University of Utah, scaled Martin Newell's teapot model by 3/4 during a demo. He liked its new shape and kept it that way. In fact, everyone liked this shorter version, including Martin Newell. Since 1976, this version of the teapot appeared in numerous publications, turning it into a symbol of computer graphics.Utah Teapot was first introduced to the computer graphics community at SIGGRAPH 1976 in an article by Jim Blinn and Martin Newell, titled “Texture and Reflection in Computer Generated Images” (PDF). It was also published in the Communications of the ACM journal and an image from this article, featuring the Utah Teapot with a texture mapped to its patches, was used as the cover of the October 1976 issue.Jim Blinn explains the components of the teapot and why it was squished in an article titled “What, Teapots Again?” (PDF), published in IEEE Computer Graphics & Applications in September 1987. There, he also suggests adding a flat bottom cap.The cover of the CACM journal in October 1976, featuring one of the images from Blinn and Newell's paper at SIGGRAPH 1976, and two other images from the same paper with the original pixels computed on PDP-11 (after tone mapping) by Jim Blinn.Version 1987 - Frank CrowThe most common version of Utah Teapot that appears in numerous graphics applications is the one released by Frank Crow, who was another PhD graduate of the University of Utah, in an article titled “The Origins of the Teapot” (PDF), published in IEEE Computer Graphics & Applications in January 1987. This article discusses the important role that the Utah Teapot model played in the early days of computer graphics and includes the control points of the scaled model by Jim Blinn. Except that all control points are shifted up just a bit to make room for a round bottom surface, defined by 4 additional Bézier patches. This brings the total number of patches to 32 and the total number of control points to 512.Crow's figure showing the patch boundaries and the control polygon of the Teapot without its body, but with the bottom that he added.Version 1992 - Hank DriskillThe handle and the spout patches of the original Utah Teapot model intersect with its body. This was necessary, as it was modeled using cubic Bézier patches. This was also a useful feature for testing various hidden surface removal algorithms that were being developed at the time, and their abilities in rendering intersecting surfaces. Also, because cubic Bézier patches cannot form perfectly circular shapes, the teapot's body was not perfectly round. Perhaps more importantly, it did not contain an interior and a rather visible gap around the lid.In 1992, Hank Driskill, another PhD student at the University of Utah, addressed all these problems. He used the Alpha_1 software, which was being developed by Professors Elaine Cohen and Rich Riesenfeld and their students/collaborators, and he prepared a trimmed NURBS model of the Utah Teapot, connecting its perfectly round body to its handle and spout, and a new interior surface. Its bottom was flat, as suggested by Jim Blinn, instead of the round bottom that was previously added by Frank Crow. Nonetheless, Hank Driskill's design, titled “Utah, the Next Generation,” featuring this new Utah Teapot (with warp nacelles), won the SIGGRAPH 1992 T-Shirt Contest.*Hank Driskill's version used a thick curve to cut a path through the spout. Here, we use the spout interior designed by Russ Fish instead.The interior of this version was defined by revolving B-spline curves, resulting in 86 additional patches, so this version of the Utah Teapot has 118 patches in total.Driskill's Teapot images with his new model and warp nacelles, and the award-winning t-shirt at SIGGRAPH 1992.The version by Hank Driskill was later improved by Russ Fish, a co-founder and technical lead of the Alpha_1 project at the University of Utah. Russ Fish modeled a new interior with a hollow knob for the lid and presented his “third-generation” teapot at SIGGRAPH 2006 with the title “Teapot Subdivision.” He also released and documented this new and earlier versions of the Utah Teapot. In particular, his solution for generating the interior of the spout is elegant and closely follows the exterior contours prepared by Martin Newell. Similar to Hank Driskill's version, this one also has a flat bottom, rather than the round bottom of Frank Crow's version.The "Teapot Subdivision" image generated by Russ Fish.This version forms even more patches to model the interior, resulting in 134 patches in total.Version 2026 - Cem YukselThe latest version of the Utah Teapot is prepared by Prof. Cem Yuksel of the University of Utah. This version uses much fewer patches for modeling the Teapot's interior and more closely follows the contours of its exterior. It contains a solid knob for the lid. The spout interior is also slightly modified to ensure that the surface normals are continuous where the tip of the spout meets the interior surface.The new interior design works with both the round bottom of Frank Crow's model and the flat bottom used by Hank Driskill and Russ Fish. The official version has a round bottom, so that it matches the most commonly used form of the Utah Teapot today.In addition, this latest version also includes two types of modifications to the exterior surface of the Utah Teapot:Its original spline models are modified using a new continuity enhancement method to ensure curvature continuity. This ensures that the reflections on the teapot appear smooth, without the sharp changes that appear in the earlier versions. See the SIGGRAPH 2026 paper on this topic by Cem Yuksel, titled “Continuity-Enhancing Degree Elevation and Splits” for more information.It also includes small chamfers where the spout and the handle meet the Teapot's body, ensuring that the teapot's surface normal is continuous over the exterior surface. The actual physical teapot that Martin Newell used as a reference has much larger chamfers, but adding such larger chamfers would deviate too much from the historical shape of the digital model.The lightweight interior model of this version only needs 30 additional patches, so the resulting teapot has 62 patches in total.Cem Yuksel also added texture mapping layouts that can be applied all versions of the Utah Teapot to achieve a bijective or a lower-distortion injective mapping.

item.content:encoded: Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one passBuilt on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer: Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate. Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.The field uses the same block format as the Interactions API.
